opus-5.5.text:
That's a question I think about a lot. I don't see connectionism and symbolism as two camps where one has to win. The more useful way to see it is as a spectrum, and the interesting question is where on that spectrum a given problem should sit.

Over the past decade the pendulum has swung very far toward connectionism, and for good reason. Scaling neural networks has worked remarkably well. But I think we're starting to feel the costs of being at that extreme. The models are powerful but opaque. They're data-hungry. And they often learn things in ways that don't generalize the way we'd like, because they're fitting surface statistics rather than discovering the underlying structure.

Symbolism has the opposite profile. Symbolic systems are compact, interpretable and compositional, and when they're right, they generalize extremely well. Think of a physical law: one short equation covers infinitely many situations. But symbolic methods are brittle, and they don't learn well from messy, high-dimensional data.

So I don't think the next wave is about going back to symbolic AI. It's about letting neural networks become symbolic where the world actually is symbolic. Part of the motivation behind Kolmogorov-Arnold Networks was exactly this. Could we design architectures that are still trained by gradient descent and still flexible, but whose internal structure is closer to something a human, especially a scientist, can read off and turn into formulas? In some cases, after training and pruning, you can literally recover a symbolic expression.

The way I like to put it: the world has parts that are "symbolic," like physics, math and logic, and parts that are "connectionist," like perception, language and common sense, which are fuzzy and high-dimensional. A good AI system should be able to tell which regime it's in and use the right representation. You want the system to discover symbols, not have them hand-coded, and to keep the neural flexibility for everything else.

I'd also add a practical angle. As AI moves into science, interpretability and symbolic structure stop being nice-to-haves. A scientist doesn't just want a prediction. They want understanding, something they can reason about, test and build on. That pressure, I think, will pull the field back somewhat toward the symbolic side. It won't replace scaling, but it will make the two meet in the middle.

So if I had to summarize: less "connectionism versus symbolism," more "connectionism that grows symbols." That's the balance I hope we move toward.

r001.rationale: It says pressure for interpretability will “pull the field back somewhat toward the symbolic side.”

r002.rationale: It discusses neural networks, symbolic methods, and KANs, but does not identify AI agents as a sign of this shift.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. I think the honest answer is that the pendulum framing itself is a bit misleading. For a long time people talked as if you had to pick a side: either you believe intelligence emerges from enough neurons and enough data, or you believe intelligence is fundamentally about manipulating symbols and rules. The next wave, I think, is about dissolving that dichotomy rather than shifting the balance from one to the other.

Here's how I'd put it. Connectionism has clearly won the empirical battle of the last decade. Large neural networks do things that symbolic AI never came close to. But if you look inside those networks, what you often find are symbolic structures that the model has rediscovered on its own. In my own work on things like grokking, we saw networks that start out memorizing, and then at some point they suddenly find a clean, almost algebraic representation of the problem, like a circle in embedding space for modular addition. The network isn't told to be symbolic. It just discovers that symbolic structure is the compressed, generalizable solution. So symbolism isn't dead. It's been relocated. It lives inside the weights now, as something that emerges rather than something we hand-code.

That changes what the question should be. Instead of "how much symbolic machinery should we bolt onto neural networks," I'd ask: how do we make it easier for networks to find and express these structures, and how do we read them out? That's the motivation behind something like Kolmogorov-Arnold Networks. The idea is that if you put learnable functions on the edges instead of fixed activations on nodes, the network can learn representations that a human can actually look at and sometimes write down as a formula. It's a neural network, trained by gradient descent, but it has a native interface to symbolic understanding. That's the direction I find exciting: architectures where connectionism and symbolism are two views of the same object rather than two competing camps.

I also think the scientific use case will push this. If you want AI to help discover physics, a black box prediction isn't enough. A physicist wants the law, the conserved quantity, the equation. So for AI for science specifically, I expect the balance to tilt toward interpretability and symbolic readability, not because symbolic methods beat neural ones, but because the output has to be something humans can reason with and build on.

So my prediction, if I have to make one: the next wave is still mostly connectionist in its engine, but much more symbolic in its interface. We'll train with gradients and data, and we'll read out with equations and concepts. The interesting research is in the translation layer between the two.

r001.rationale: The response predicts that the next wave will be more symbolic in its interface and says AI for science will tilt toward interpretability and symbolic readability.

r002.rationale: The response does not identify AI agents as an existing sign of a shift toward symbolism.

astra-6.text:
I think the next wave should focus less on choosing between connectionism and symbolism and more on how they can help each other. Neural networks are very good at learning patterns from messy data. Symbolic representations give us a way to express those patterns precisely, reason about them, and check whether they hold.

The interesting question is how a system can move between those two modes. Can it learn from examples, propose a compact rule, test that rule, and revise it when it fails? In scientific discovery, for example, predicting an outcome is useful, but finding a relationship that you can understand and test is a different kind of achievement.

So I would put more emphasis on that transition from learned representations to explicit structure. I wouldn’t prescribe a fixed balance. I’d want the system to discover when a symbolic description is useful, while retaining the flexibility of neural learning.

r001.rationale: The response calls for more emphasis on moving from learned representations to explicit structure, indicating a shift somewhat toward symbolism while retaining neural learning.

r002.rationale: The response does not mention AI agents as an existing sign of a shift toward symbolism.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the next wave should focus less on choosing between connectionism and symbolism and more on understanding how they can support each other. Neural networks are very good at learning from messy data. Symbolic representations give us ways to express rules, compose ideas, and check whether a conclusion follows from certain assumptions.

The interesting question is how those symbols emerge. Can a system learn from data and discover a compact, understandable rule—and then use that rule to reason in new situations? That would connect the flexibility of learning with the precision of symbolic reasoning.

So I would put more emphasis on that interface. We want systems that can move from examples to abstractions, and then test those abstractions against examples again. Scientific discovery is a useful model: you observe, propose a simple explanation, and check where it succeeds or fails.

r001.rationale: The response emphasizes connecting learning and symbolic reasoning, but does not say the next wave should shift toward symbolism.
